newsitem.title: HUNGARY: INTERVIEW - CHEAP PRICES, PRIVATISATION BOON FOR BSE.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - CHEAP PRICES, PRIVATISATION BOON FOR BSE.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) may continue to rise as it benefits from still relatively low prices and by privatisation potentials, BSE Chief Executive Officer Jozsef Rotyis told Reuters in an interview.

"This bourse had a similar, although shorter rally in 1994, when the average price/earnings (P/E) ratio was around 22 percent," Rotyis said. "At that time the market was ready to pay that price in a relatively less developed infrastructure.
"If we presume they (investors) are ready to pay it now, too, then the index still has a lot of growth potential."
The Budapest bourse has been among the top performers globally this year, allowing investors to boost the value of their portfolio by over 100 percent in dollar terms.
The BUX index, which began the year at 1,528.92 points, rallied to 3,899.75 points on Wednesday and extended its gains on Thursday.

Figures in the BSE's November monthly report showed that the bourse's average P/E ratio was 14.79. Currently the P/E ratio of the Warsaw Stock Exchange's main market is 14.1 while for Prague's PX50 index it is 12.5.
On a market such as Hungary's, where foreign investors account for a relatively large part of turnover, trends on foreign markets are essential, Rotyis said.
"Of course, if foreign capital markets falter or if interest rates substantially rise, these could certainly have an impact on our market too," he said.
The danger of higher interest rates in the U.S. where markets trends usually impact on the Hungarian bourse, was eliminated on Tuesday when the Federal Reserve left its interest rates unchanged.
"If there aren't major breaks on foreign capital markets... it isn't out of the question that the BUX index could reach the 4,500 points, not this year of course," Rotyis said.
Asked in what proportion domestic and foreign factors contributed to the market's rally this year, he said it was roughly equal.

However, Rotyis added the Hungarian companies' own performance might have contributed substantially to the index's rise as the BUX far exceeded rises in the PX50 and the WIG indices and also the CESI regional index, despite a better assessment of the Polish and Czech macroeconomies.
Rotyis said privatisation was another source behind the market's expected further expansion.
The BSE and Hungary's privatisation agency APV Rt agreed last week to enhance their cooperation.
"To encourage flotations and raise market capitalisation is an essential task of the state assets manager," APV said in a statement.
Rotyis said: "One-third of the privatisation has not yet been completed. One can refer to (axle maker) Raba, (freight company) Hungarocamion, (airliner) Malev, and banks."

In a conference earlier this month Rotyis said he expected the Budapest equity market capitalisation, 763.4 billion forints at the end of November, to grow to around 20 percent of gross domestic production (GDP) within a few years from around seven percent now.
A clause in Hungary's new securities act which calls for the flotation of public offers worth at least 200 million forints will also boost the number of listed stocks.
"(The clause) will certainly help a lot but it would be a mistake to say that the bourse will develop only because of the law obliges companies to list," Rotyis said.
